title: Inside the Reform — what Verne got right
learning_goal: Know the Reform Club is real, founded 1836, Barry's palazzo of 1841, Soyer's kitchens, and Fogg's breakfast; feel cosy club warmth.

narration.script: We arrive at the door of Fogg's club. The Reform Club is real, and still here: 104 Pall Mall. Its founders backed the great Reform Act of 1832 — hence the name. In the novel this is Fogg's whole world: he eats here, reads here, plays cards here, every day until midnight. Charles Barry's palazzo opened in 1841: Portland stone outside, and inside, the saloon. And the famous kitchens that the chef Alexis Soyer helped to plan. Look down — they ran in the basement, under all this. Now Fogg's breakfast, taken here. A broiled fish with Reading sauce — keep that in mind. Inside today: a tessellated floor, marble busts, portraits between the columns. Barry's elevation of the front. Somewhere in there, breakfast done, Fogg cuts the pages himself and reads The Times.

variants.clear: This is the door of Fogg's club: the Reform Club. It is real, and still here — 104 Pall Mall. Its founders had backed the Reform Act of 1832 — that is where the name comes from. In the book, Fogg spends every day here until midnight: meals, newspapers, cards. The architect Charles Barry finished the building in 1841. Stone outside; inside, this hall. The club also had famous kitchens, planned with the chef Alexis Soyer. They were down in the basement. Here Fogg ate his breakfast: grilled fish with Reading sauce — remember that sauce. Then Barry's design for the front. Somewhere in there, Fogg cuts his newspaper's pages and reads The Times.

M-20 (File:Facade_of_The_Reform_Club..._6571401, Philip Cornwall, geograph 2019) is a fine photograph of the club that happens to have been taken during a Brexit demonstration — EU flags on poles and hand-painted placards with legible slogans occupy the lower half of the frame. It opened this scene, was the fallback still in scene 04 and sat (inertly) in scene 07, so contemporary politics recurred three times through a chapter set in 1872; brief.md's must-not list excludes exactly that. Chosen instead: M-105, Phil Guest's 2014 low-angle photograph of the Reform Club's own doorway (4896x3672, CC BY-SA 2.0) — the door, in a picture with no people, no signage and no flag on the pole. It was chosen per-slot against the sentence, not globally: the clear track's first two sentences are 'This is the door of Fogg's club: the Reform Club. It is real, and still here — 104 Pall Mall', and this picture is literally both halves of that. The alternatives the founder had fetched were both considered and both rejected FOR THIS SLOT: M-102 (Barry 1867 wood engraving) is the club as Fogg saw it but is not a door, carries no 'still here', and would put a second engraving of this same elevation on screen 42 s before M-22 does; M-21 (the polished 104 PALL MALL plaque, 2448x2448) matches the address word for word but is square — a heavy pillarbox in 16:9 — and gives a first-time viewer no building to stand in front of at the top of a scene. Identification of M-105 is firm: Phil Guest photographed the 104 plaque (M-21) at 11:25:59 and this doorway at 11:26:16 on 20 September 2014, both titled 'The Reform Club, London', and the doorcase, console brackets and Greek-fret band match the 1867 engraving M-102 and the 2015 photograph M-104. Nothing else in the scene changed: slot windows, narration, overlays, the four interiors and the closing 1841 engraving are as A10 left them.
